ads.headline: Ce que j'ai changé à 62 ans
ads.primaryText:
J'ai 62 ans. Ces trois derniers mois, mon mari pense que j'ai maigri, ma fille croit que je me suis « fait faire quelque chose », et ma kiné m'a demandé ce que j'avais changé.
Je n'ai rien fait de tout ça. J'ai juste arrêté de porter un soutien-gorge qui me serrait — et j'ai trouvé autre chose.
Pendant des années, j'ai cru que la gêne faisait partie du lot : les marques rouges le soir, la bande qui roule sous les bras, l'agrafe qu'on sent dans le dos. On finit par s'y habituer. On ne se rend même plus compte à quel point on est mal.
Une amie m'a parlé du Débardeur Signature de Belle Simone. Un débardeur avec un vrai soutien intégré : la poitrine est tenue par l'avant, sans armature ni compression. La matière est si douce qu'on l'oublie, et la silhouette est lissée — sans rien qui creuse.
La première fois que je l'ai mis, j'ai compris la différence en dix secondes. Plus de marques le soir. Plus de geste pour réajuster. Et, visiblement, une allure qui se voit.
Il existe du 38 au 54, pensé pour toutes les morphologies. Si tant de femmes l'ont adopté, ce n'est pas un hasard.
👉 Le maintien d'un soutien-gorge, le confort d'un débardeur. Essai 45 jours.

ads.headline: post-mastectomy? read this...☝️
ads.primaryText:
I spent three years getting dressed in the dark so I wouldn't have to see my own chest in the mirror.

My name is Marta. I'm 62.

I had a single mastectomy three years ago, and I chose not to reconstruct.

I was done with surgery. I just wanted to feel like myself again without going back under.

Turns out the whole world is built for a body I no longer had.

Every bra I owned assumed I had two breasts to fill it. The cups gaped on the side that was gone.

My old camisoles hung off my chest like they were still waiting for a body that wasn't coming back.

Fitted shirts were the worst, so I stopped wearing them and lived in cardigans and loose tunics that swallowed me whole.

And the usual fix was its own misery.

A loose silicone form you wrestle into a stiff pocketed bra. A band wrapping your ribs. Underwire that finds your scar by lunchtime.

Then there were the comments. Not cruel ones. That would almost have been easier.

The soft, pitying ones. The tilted head. The "have you thought about reconstruction."

Like my body was a question I kept answering wrong.

About a year in, I joined an online group for women who'd had mastectomies.

I wasn't looking to buy anything. I just wanted to be around people who understood that I wasn't grieving my old body.

I just wanted clothes that fit the one I actually live in now.

That's where I saw the post.

A woman named Amy had put up a photo of herself in a plain tank top, smooth and even across the chest. No gaping. No bunching.

She looked comfortable. She looked like herself.
The comments filled up fast. What is that. Where is it from. Does it actually stay put.

Amy said it was a tank called Velcy.

The support is built into the front of the fabric, not a band strangling your ribs. No underwire.

And it comes with soft forms already sewn inside, so the shape is just there the moment you put it on. No loose prosthetic to fight into a bra. If you want more shape, you can add to them.

She said it was the first thing she'd found that gave her a natural shape without treating her chest like a problem to fix.

I ordered one that night. I didn't expect much. I'd been let down too many times.

When it came, the first thing I noticed was what I didn't feel.

No band cutting into my ribs. No wire. No pressure anywhere near my scar.

The support sat soft across the front, and the shape was already there, even and natural under my shirt.
Nothing to insert. Nothing to adjust.

I walked around the house for a while, reaching and bending the way I move through a normal day.
Nothing shifted. Nothing rode up. It just stayed.

Then I put on a fitted shirt. The kind I hadn't worn in three years.

And when I looked in the mirror I didn't see someone hiding, and I didn't see someone apologizing.
I saw a shape that looked like mine. I saw me.

I want to be honest about what this is.

Velcy is not a medical device, and I'm not going to tell you it fixes anything.

It's a wire-free tank with the support built into the front and soft, durable forms already sewn inside, so you get a natural, even shape the moment you put it on.
If you want more shape, you can add to the forms. If you reconstructed, it sits soft over tender skin with nothing pressing on a scar.

The fabric is soft, the straps are wide enough not to dig, and there's no band around your back, so you stay smooth under anything you wear.

They're running an offer right now with a guarantee, so if it isn't right for you, you send it back and you're out nothing.

You can see it here: https://www.velcy.co/products/velcy-built-in-bra-comfort-shaper-tank

I don't know who's reading this.

But if you said no to more surgery and still want to feel like yourself in your own clothes, if you're tired of products that treat your chest like something to solve, I'll just say this.

Cancer already took enough. It doesn't get to take getting dressed too.

I spent three years getting dressed in the dark so I wouldn't have to see my own chest in the mirror.

My name is Marta. I'm 62.

I had a single mastectomy three years ago, and I chose not to reconstruct.

I was done with surgery. I just wanted to feel like myself again without going back under.

Turns out the whole world is built for a body I no longer had.

Every bra I owned assumed I had two breasts to fill it. The cups gaped on the side that was gone.

My old camisoles hung off my chest like they were still waiting for a body that wasn't coming back.

Fitted shirts were the worst, so I stopped wearing them and lived in cardigans and loose tunics that swallowed me whole.

And the usual fix was its own misery.

A loose silicone form you wrestle into a stiff pocketed bra. A band wrapping your ribs. Underwire that finds your scar by lunchtime.

Then there were the comments. Not cruel ones. That would almost have been easier.

The soft, pitying ones. The tilted head. The "have you thought about reconstruction."

Like my body was a question I kept answering wrong.

About a year in, I joined an online group for women who'd had mastectomies.

I wasn't looking to buy anything. I just wanted to be around people who understood that I wasn't grieving my old body.

I just wanted clothes that fit the one I actually live in now.

That's where I saw the post.

A woman named Amy had put up a photo of herself in a plain tank top, smooth and even across the chest. No gaping. No bunching.

She looked comfortable. She looked like herself.
The comments filled up fast. What is that. Where is it from. Does it actually stay put.

Amy said it was a tank called Wellvi.

The support is built into the front of the fabric, not a band strangling your ribs. No underwire.

And it comes with soft forms already sewn inside, so the shape is just there the moment you put it on. No loose prosthetic to fight into a bra. If you want more shape, you can add to them.

She said it was the first thing she'd found that gave her a natural shape without treating her chest like a problem to fix.

I ordered one that night. I didn't expect much. I'd been let down too many times.

When it came, the first thing I noticed was what I didn't feel.

No band cutting into my ribs. No wire. No pressure anywhere near my scar.

The support sat soft across the front, and the shape was already there, even and natural under my shirt.
Nothing to insert. Nothing to adjust.

I walked around the house for a while, reaching and bending the way I move through a normal day.
Nothing shifted. Nothing rode up. It just stayed.

Then I put on a fitted shirt. The kind I hadn't worn in three years.

And when I looked in the mirror I didn't see someone hiding, and I didn't see someone apologizing.
I saw a shape that looked like mine. I saw me.

I want to be honest about what this is.

Wellvi is not a medical device, and I'm not going to tell you it fixes anything.

It's a wire-free tank with the support built into the front and soft, durable forms already sewn inside, so you get a natural, even shape the moment you put it on.
If you want more shape, you can add to the forms. If you reconstructed, it sits soft over tender skin with nothing pressing on a scar.

The fabric is soft, the straps are wide enough not to dig, and there's no band around your back, so you stay smooth under anything you wear.

They're running an offer right now with a guarantee, so if it isn't right for you, you send it back and you're out nothing.

You can see it here: https://get.trywellvi.com/pages/bras-forever

I don't know who's reading this.

But if you said no to more surgery and still want to feel like yourself in your own clothes, if you're tired of products that treat your chest like something to solve, I'll just say this.

Cancer already took enough. It doesn't get to take getting dressed too.

ads.headline: post-mastectomy? read this...☝️
ads.primaryText:
Don't buy another mastectomy bra until you hear what happened to my 81-year-old client.

Look, I've been a certified mastectomy fitter for 24 years.

I've fitted thousands of women in that little room with the fluorescent light and the curtain that never quite closes...

And for 24 years I handed them the same thing. A pocketed bra. A silicone form. "This is the best we have."

But it was only when my 81-year-old client, the one I see at water aerobics on Tuesdays, told me she'd quit the class that I finally admitted something was wrong.

Her prosthesis weighs about a pound and a half. Twenty-six years she carried it.

She'd tried every bra in my fitting room. The $85 ones. The front-closure ones. The "seamless comfort" ones.

Some helped a little. Not enough.

And she wasn't the only one.

Hundreds of women sat in my fitting room and asked me the same question...

"Is it supposed to be this uncomfortable? or Is it me?"

But here's where it gets interesting.

When a woman came to me because her bra rode up, shifted, and left grooves in her shoulders, the problem was almost never her body.

The problem was the engineering.

A bra is a hanging system. It's built to hang weight from the shoulders and anchor it with a tight band around the ribs.

That design assumes two things are still there to balance the load.

After a mastectomy, on one side or both, the geometry the bra was designed around is gone.

So the band climbs. The form drifts. The straps dig into the shoulder, often the exact side where lymph nodes were removed. The wire presses right on scar tissue that never fully stopped being tender.

Her body was never the problem. The bra was never engineered for her body.

It's worse for some women:

One side is still there, so all the weight hangs uneven
The prosthesis is heavy, a pound or more
The skin around the scar is thin or radiated
Reaching back for a clasp stopped being easy after surgery
Now, if the hanging design is the real culprit...

Then the fix is not a better version of the same bra.

Support has to come from the FRONT, resting on the torso, not hanging off the shoulders.

I learned this when my water-aerobics client showed up in a tank top and asked me to guess what was under it.

Nothing was under it. It WAS the bra.

A tank with a double-layer front panel, soft cups sewn inside, and a pocket at chest level on each side. Her prosthesis sat in the pocket on her flat side. The support came from the front panel, not from straps.

She'd been wearing it for two weeks. The grooves in her shoulders were fading. She was back at aerobics that Tuesday.

In 24 years of fittings I had never seen a woman turn around that fast.

I ordered three to test on my own clients. Same story, again and again. The women who used to cry in my fitting room came back. Not with complaints. To ask for colors.

Now... how does it actually work?

The weight rests on the front of your torso, spread across a double-layer panel. Nothing hangs from your shoulders. Nothing clamps around your ribs. Nothing touches the scar line the way a band does.

The soft cups are sewn in, so you can wear it completely flat, with the light forms that come included, or drop your own prosthesis into the side pockets. Single, double, it works the same.

And it goes on over your head in about 3 seconds. No clasp behind your back.

The only one I now recommend is the tank from a company called Velcy, and here's why.

Since these took off, copycats have flooded in. Women bring them to my fitting room. Thin single-layer nylon. A little slit in the middle that a real prosthesis cannot physically fit through. No forms in the box.

They do this to make more money.

The real Velcy has the pockets on the SIDES, sized for an actual prosthesis, a true double-layer front, and the soft forms already included.

On top of that, it comes with a 90-day money-back guarantee and free exchanges.

That's why they can show a 4.9 out of 5 rating from more than 12,325 women.

Before I wrote this, I contacted Velcy and told them what I was seeing in my fitting room.

So they set up a link with their summer deal, the first one they've ever run. Buy 2, get 1 free, with cooling pads included for the hot months.

Here are the patterns I see in the first 4 weeks, from the women I fit:

✅ Week 1: it goes on in 3 seconds every morning. The bathroom-mirror checking starts to stop.

✅ Week 2: the shoulder grooves start fading. No more reaching in to reposition anything.

✅ Week 3: the fitted tops come out of the back of the closet.

✅ Week 4: they come back. Not with a complaint. To buy 2 more and one for a friend from their support group.

This is the link my clients use:

👉 https://www.velcy.co/products/velcy-built-in-bra-comfort-shaper-tank

Sizes run S to 3XL and the popular ones have sold out more than once this summer, so if yours is there, don't sit on it.

And remember the 90 days. Wear it. Do the aerobics class. See if the grooves fade. If you don't feel a difference, they give you every penny back.

After 24 years of handing women bras that needed an apology with them, this is the first thing I hand over that doesn't.

If your size is available, get it. You'll be glad you did.
